lines.text: Ten o'clock at night. Shanti Nagar, Mumbai.
The river is rising. And every phone in the ward is calling for help.
पानी घुटनों तक आ गया है, पोते को बुखार है… गली चार, हनुमान मंदिर के पीछे
lines.caption: “The water is up to our knees, my grandson has a fever… Lane 4, behind the Hanuman temple.”

lines.text: Here is the problem, in two sentences.
In a flood, a control room gets hundreds of messages at once: the same family three times, rumours, and voice notes in three languages.
So boats go out in the order calls arrive, and the families in the most danger wait the longest.
On our test night, that was almost eight hours.
lines.caption: On our test night, that was almost eight hours. (463 minutes)

lines.text: This is Pukaar. Every call heard. Every family reached.
Built by Team Seekers.
Pukaar works like a team of seven small helpers. Each one does one job, and none of them can send a boat on its own.
Listen reads every message, even a voice note in Hindi, and pulls out what matters: who is there, how deep the water is, and who is sick.
Triage sees that three messages are about the same house, merges them into one ticket, and ranks it by need, with the reasons written out.
Dispatch picks the nearest boat with a medic, and plans a route around blocked roads.
Then a person decides. The duty officer. One tap: approve.
Loop tells the family, in their own language, that help is coming, with a code so the crew knows they reached the right door.
Saathi answers safety questions, Watch reads weather alerts, and Planner keeps every step on record.
Let's watch it work, live. The officer signs in to the control room.
Kamla's grandson has a fever. She sends a message from her phone, in Hindi.
Within seconds it's on the control room screen. Then her daughter writes from Pune, and a neighbour writes too. Pukaar folds all three into one ticket.
Priority one, with the reasons spelled out, and the raw messages one tap away.
Boat 1 has a medic and is eleven minutes away. The officer checks the route, and approves.
The crew accepts on their phone, and at that same moment, Kamla's phone lights up: the boat is coming, and here is your code.
At the door, the family reads out the code. Confirmed. Safe.
A forwarded message says a dam has burst? It goes to Verify, not to a boat.
Someone smells gas? Saathi replies with the emergency number first, one nine zero six, and safe steps.
lines.caption: Someone smells gas? Saathi replies with the emergency number first, 1906, and safe steps.

lines.text: A crew reports a flooded lane, and every boat routed through it is sent another way.
The officer can open the family chat or the lookup right inside the control room.
And a worried relative can check on a family, and see only one thing: rescued, and safe at Camp 3. Never an address. Never a phone number.
Here's a whole flood night, playing at ten times speed. Three hundred and eleven messages.
The queue ranks itself, the map fills in, and the officer only sees what needs a human decision.
Safety is built in, not bolted on.
Agents can raise a priority, but never lower it. No boat and no public bulletin goes out without approval. Every action is logged with a name. And one switch stops all automation, instantly.
Under the hood, it's simple on purpose.
Every agent lives in its own file. Agents never touch the world directly; they call small tools, and the tools enforce the rules.
A Python FastAPI backend with SQLite, and a live event stream to every screen. A React, Tailwind and Leaflet frontend: one app for the control room, the family's phone, and the boat crew.
It runs on a single laptop. With no AI model at all, or a local model through Ollama, so messages never leave the ward.
Here is the rule that matters most, in real code. An agent asks for approval, and the system refuses to act until a person says yes.
Every safety rule has a test. All sixty seven pass.
We replayed that full flood night against the usual way: first come, first served.
Time to send a boat to the most urgent families fell from four hundred and sixty three minutes, to twenty.
Wasted trips fell from one hundred and thirty one to fifteen. And every one of the fifteen rumours was caught.
And floods are just the start.
Swap the map and the playbooks, and the same agents can handle other disasters.

A cyclone: Watch moves boats before landfall. An earthquake: Triage ranks people trapped under rubble. A heatwave: Saathi sends people to the nearest cooling centre. A fire: Dispatch routes around the smoke.
Pukaar means, a call for help. We make sure every one is answered.
Team Seekers.
